https://www.politico.eu/article/swedens-.text: Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson resigned after narrowly losing a closely fought election, paving the way for a new center-left government to take over. Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson is now expected to begin formal negotiations with other parties in her bloc and, if she can get a deal, she will become Sweden’s new prime minister in the weeks ahead. “The Swedish people have voted for a new direction for our country,” Andersson said in a video posted on social media. She said the election showed voters wanted “cohesion” and not “division” and promised to work for unity as prime minister. Advertisement Advertisement Anderson said she would seek to prioritize a fair migration system that stops unfair deportations, a climate policy that sees green transition as an opportunity for Sweden, better elderly care and healthcare, and a revitalized economy to boost growth and reduce unemployment. The contest offered voters a choice between Andersson’s center-left and socialist alliance of four parties, and Kristersson’s rightwing grouping of four parties, which included the far-right anti-immigration Sweden Democrats. During the campaign, Andersson, who previously served as prime minister until the 2022 election, warned voters against handing power to the Sweden Democrats after Kristersson said he would offer the far-right party ministerial jobs in his next government. But the result capped a bad election for the Sweden Democrats who were hoping to enter power as for the first time but lost votes, seats and influence instead. The Swedish Election Authority’s final tally of the preliminary vote count gives Andersson’s left bloc 176 seats to Kristersson’s 173. Despite winning the most seats, Andersson still needs the support of the three other parties in her leftwing bloc to achieve a majority. Advertisement Advertisement That may not be easy as two of these potential allies are at odds: The Left Party has named its price as having ministers in the government — and that’s something the liberal Center Party says it cannot accept. Andersson said “a new era of cooperation between the political parties” would be needed. In his resignation letter to the speaker of parliament, Kristersson, the conservative center-right leader, appealed for talks between “all parties” because pre-existing red lines would make finding a coalition hard. Although he didn’t name Andersson or the dispute between the Green and Left parties, it’s likely that he had these issues in mind. “A constructive openness will now be needed from the parties in the Riksdag for a prime minister to be tolerated — and for a new government to gain support for its state budget,” Kristersson wrote. “Talks will need to be held with all parties to find ways around these deadlocks and create the conditions for a stable and effective government.” One option sometimes discussed by commentators in Sweden is for the main center left and center right parties — Andersson’s Social Democrats and Kristersson’s Moderates — to come together to form a grand coalition, removing the need for support from either end of the political spectrum. But even if they did agree to work together, these two parties would still need backing from a third to get a majority, and collaboration between the two rival camps is seen as highly unlikely by political insiders. Negotiations could last weeks. The earliest a new prime minister can be sworn in is Sept. 29. Barring an unlikely unravelling of those negotiations, the result heralds the end of conservative Kristersson’s hopes of holding onto his job. He is expected to take a caretaker role until a new government is formed. This article was updated. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-apologizes.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ONlR Italian Eurofighters operating under NATO command were scrambled in response to the drone incident in Lithuania (FILE 04/03/2024) Image: Armando Babani/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Ukraine apologized Sunday after a suspected drone crashed in northern Lithuania , prompting shelter warnings and the deployment of NATO fighter jets. The incident raised fresh concerns about the spillover of Russia's war against Ukraine into NATO territory, although the drone's origin and whether it carried explosives remained under investigation. What happened in Lithuania? Lithuanian authorities told residents in central and northern regions to seek shelter Sunday morning after detecting an unidentified flying object. Debris damaged a moving civilian vehicle, but no one was injured, national crisis management centre chief Vilmantas Vitkauskas told Lithuanian radio. Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said the drone probably entered from neighboring Poland. He proposed a joint investigation with Warsaw. Lithuanian PM warns of Russian nuclear threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Two Italian Eurofighter jets operating under NATO command were deployed, a NATO spokesperson said. Kaunas said weather conditions prevented visual identification. Have similar incidents happened before? Lithuania and its Baltic neighbors have experienced several drone incursions during the war. Ukrainian drones intended to strike targets in northwestern Russia have previously strayed into Baltic airspace and crashed. Russian-made drones have also entered Lithuania from Belarus . Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda described Sunday's incident as another example of the war spilling onto NATO's eastern flank. Meanwhile, Lithuania said it was treating an attempted arson attack on a Starlink base station near Vilnius as Russia-linked sabotage aimed at undermining Ukraine's military capacity. National crisis management chief Vilmantas Vitkauskas said Sunday that authorities were searching for suspects who tried to set fire to the facility at about 2 a.m. (2300 GMT Saturday). https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/07/we-w.text: US President Donald Trump said he “will definitely look” into the possibility of opening a permanenert US base in Lithuania — the Baltic country at the eastern NATO flank. “They are friends of mine, they are great people. So we will certainly look at it,” Trump told LRT reporter when asked whether US would consider establishing a permanent military base in Lithuania. The comments follow Lithuania’s Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius conversation with John Coale, President Donald Trump’s envoy to neighbouring Belarus, where he told that Vilnius wants US troops to be permanently stationed in the Baltic country amid Russia’s war in Ukraine and a series of hybrid threats, including drone incursions and the instrumentalization of migration by Belarus. “I am very happy that such idea is not rejected by President Trump,” Sinkevičius said in a Facebook post on Tuesday. “We are ready to provide the best possible conditions for the US.”He tasked Lithuania’s defence ministry “to do their homeworks” — to present opportunities and conditions under which Lithuania could be welcoming US soldiers. Around a 1,000 US soldiers are due to arrive in Lithuania at the end of October as part of a rotational deployment. They are expected to serve in the country for nine months. American soldiers also are deployed on rotational bases also in Estonia and Poland.Poland is already on itLithuania’s push for a permanent US presence follows a similar move by neighbouring Poland.Marcin Przydacz, head of Polish President Karol Nawrocki’s International Policy Office, said last week that White House has already given a “green light” for a permanent US base in Poland, which “now provides space for executive and subcontracting actions by the Government.”Lithuania is also to host a German brigade of around 5,000 troops by the end of 2027. Germany has, however, faced difficulties in finding enough personnel willing to serve in Lithuania. “The German brigade in Lithuania is not only a military capability—it is a clear demonstration of our Allies’ determination to defend NATO’s eastern flank,” Sinkevičius said on Wednesday, during a visit to Berlin where he met with German Federal Minister of Defence Boris Pistorius. The Prime Minister said Lithuania would meet all its commitments on schedule and create all the necessary conditions for the deployment of a combat-ready brigade by the end of 2027.
